nodes.name: Broadcast model
nodes.statement: In the \emph{broadcast} model, each sensor can broadcast a message to all other sensors at unit cost.

nodes.name: Star network model
nodes.statement: In the \emph{star network} model, messages can only be between a sensor and the base station, and each message has unit cost.

nodes.name: Set of sensor locations $V$
nodes.statement: Suppose a network of sensors has been deployed at a set of locations $V$ with the task of monitoring some phenomenon (e.g., temperature in a building).

nodes.name: Probabilistic sensor model $P({\mathcal{X}}_{V})$
nodes.statement: For example, prior work \cite{vldb04} has considered the setting where a random variable ${\mathcal{X}}_{s}$ is associated with every location $s\in V$, and a joint probability distribution $P({\mathcal{X}}_{V})$ models the correlation between sensor values.
nodes.statement_short: Each location $s$ carries a random variable ${\mathcal{X}}_s$; a joint distribution models correlations between sensor values.

nodes.name: Mean squared prediction error (MSE)
nodes.statement: One way to quantify the predictive uncertainty is the mean squared prediction error, $$\mathrm{MSE}({\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid {\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}) = \frac{1}{\ensuremath{n}}\sum_{s\in V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}} \mathbb{E}[({\mathcal{X}}_s-\mathbb{E}[{\mathcal{X}}_{s}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}])^{2}\mid {\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}].$$
nodes.statement_short: MSE: average posterior variance of the unobserved locations given observations at ${\mathcal{A}}$.

nodes.name: Expected mean squared prediction error (EMSE)
nodes.statement: Thus, we can base our optimization on the \emph{expected mean squared prediction error}, $$\mathrm{EMSE}({\mathcal{A}}) = \int dp({\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}) \mathrm{MSE}({\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid {\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}).$$
nodes.statement_short: EMSE averages the MSE over the unknown measurements ${\mathbf{x}}_{\mathcal{A}}$.

nodes.name: Variance reduction objective $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$
nodes.statement: Equivalently, we can maximize the \emph{reduction} in mean squared prediction error, $$f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}({\mathcal{A}}) = \mathrm{EMSE}(\emptyset)-\mathrm{EMSE}({\mathcal{A}}).$$
nodes.statement_short: $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$ is the reduction in EMSE relative to selecting no sensors.

nodes.name: $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$ is normalized
nodes.statement: By definition, $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}(\emptyset)=0$, i.e., no sensors obtain no utility.
conclusions: $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}(\emptyset)=0$

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$
nodes.statement: Furthermore, $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$ is monotonic: if ${\mathcal{A}}\subseteq{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq V$, then $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}({\mathcal{A}})\leq f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}({\mathcal{B}})$, i.e., adding more sensors always helps.
assumptions: ${\mathcal{A}}\subseteq{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq V$
conclusions:
$f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}({\mathcal{A}})\leq
 f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}({\mathcal{B}})$

nodes.name: Offline cardinality-constrained sensor selection
nodes.statement: However, in practice, we would like to only select a small set of, e.g., at most $k$ sensors due to bandwidth and power constraints: $${\mathcal{A}}^*=\mathop{\rm arg\,max}_{{\mathcal{A}}}f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}({\mathcal{A}})\text{ s.t. }|{\mathcal{A}}|\leq k.$$
nodes.statement_short: Choose at most $k$ sensors maximizing $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$.

nodes.name: NP-hardness of offline sensor selection
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, this optimization problem is NP-hard, so we cannot expect to efficiently find the optimal solution.
conclusions: this optimization problem is NP-hard

nodes.name: Submodularity of $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$ (Das & Kempe)
nodes.statement: Fortunately, it can be shown \cite{das07} that in many settings\footnote{For Gaussian models and conditional suppressorfreeness \cite{das07}}, the function $f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$ satisfies an intuitive diminishing returns property called submodularity.
assumptions: in many settings
conclusions:
the function
$f_{\mathrm{EMSE}}$ satisfies an intuitive diminishing returns property called
submodularity

nodes.name: Submodular set function
nodes.statement: A set function $f:2^{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is called \emph{submodular} if, for all ${\mathcal{A}}\subseteq{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq V$ and $s\in V\setminus {\mathcal{B}}$ it holds that $f({\mathcal{A}}\cup\{s\})-f({\mathcal{A}})\geq f({\mathcal{B}}\cup\{s\})-f({\mathcal{B}})$.
differentia:
for all
${\mathcal{A}}\subseteq{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq V$ and $s\in V\setminus {\mathcal{B}}$ it
holds that $f({\mathcal{A}}\cup\{s\})-f({\mathcal{A}})\geq f({\mathcal{B}}\cup\{s\})-f({\mathcal{B}})$
nodes.statement_short: Diminishing returns: adding $s$ to a smaller set helps at least as much as adding it to a larger set.

nodes.name: Sensing region model
nodes.statement: For example, the \emph{sensing region} model where $\ensuremath{f}_{REG}({\mathcal{A}})$ is the total area covered by all sensors ${\mathcal{A}}$ is submodular.

nodes.name: Detection model
nodes.statement: The \emph{detection} model where $\ensuremath{f}_{DET}({\mathcal{A}})$ counts the expected number of targets detected by sensors ${\mathcal{A}}$ is submodular as well.

nodes.name: Greedy $(1-1/e)$ approximation for monotone submodular maximization (Nemhauser et al.)
nodes.statement: A fundamental result of Nemhauser et al.~\cite{nemhauser78} is that for monotone submodular functions, a simple greedy algorithm, which starts with the empty set ${\mathcal{A}}_{0}=\emptyset$ and iteratively adds the element $$s_{k}=\mathop{\rm arg\,max}_{s\in V\setminus {\mathcal{A}}_{k-1}} f({\mathcal{A}}_{k-1}\cup\{s\});\ \ {\mathcal{A}}_{k}={\mathcal{A}}_{k-1}\cup\{s_{k}\}$$ which maximally improves the utility obtains a near-optimal solution: For the set ${\mathcal{A}}_{k}$ it holds that $$f({\mathcal{A}}_{k})\geq (1-1/e)\max_{|{\mathcal{A}}|\leq k}f({\mathcal{A}}),$$ i.e., the greedy solution obtains at least a constant fraction of $(1-1/e)\approx 63\%$ of the optimal value.
assumptions: for monotone submodular functions
conclusions: $$f({\mathcal{A}}_{k})\geq (1-1/e)\max_{|{\mathcal{A}}|\leq k}f({\mathcal{A}}),$$
nodes.statement_short: The greedy algorithm that repeatedly adds the element of largest marginal gain achieves a $(1-1/e)$ fraction of the optimum.

nodes.name: Number of rounds $T$
nodes.statement: We assume that we intend to monitor the environment for a number $T$ of time steps (rounds).

nodes.name: Selected set $S_t$
nodes.statement: In each round $t$, a set $S_{t}$ of sensors is selected, and these sensors transmit their measurements to a server (base station).

nodes.name: Sensing quality $f_t$
nodes.statement: The server then determines a sensing quality $\ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$ quantifying the utility obtained from the resulting analysis.

nodes.name: Spatial prediction feedback
nodes.statement: For example, if our goal is spatial prediction, the server would build a model based on the previously collected sensor data, pick a random sensor $s$, make prediction for the variable ${\mathcal{X}}_{s}$, and then compare the prediction $\mu_{s}$ with the sensor reading $x_{s}$. The error $\ensuremath{f}_{t}=\sigma_{s}^{2}-(\mu_{s}-x_{s})^{2}$ is an unbiased estimate of the reduction in EMSE.
nodes.statement_short: Predict a random sensor's reading; the error-based quantity is an unbiased estimate of EMSE reduction.

nodes.name: Bounded monotone submodular objectives
nodes.statement: In the following analysis, we will only assume that the objective functions $\ensuremath{f}_{t}$ are bounded (w.l.o.g., take values in $[0,1]$), monotone, and submodular, and that we have some way of computing $\ensuremath{f}_{t}(S)$ for any subset of sensors $S$.

nodes.name: Online sensor selection
nodes.statement: Our goal is to maximize the total reward obtained by the system over $T$ rounds, $\sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximize cumulative reward $\sum_t f_t(S_t)$ over $T$ rounds.

nodes.name: Regret and no-regret
nodes.statement: We thus compare our protocol against all strategies that can select a fixed set of $\ensuremath{k}$ sensors for use in all of the rounds; the best such strategy obtains reward $\max_{S \subseteq V: |S| \le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S)$. The difference between this quantity and what our protocol obtains is known as its \emph{regret}, and an algorithm is said to be \emph{no-regret} if its average regret tends to zero (or less)\footnote{Formally, if $R_T$ is the total regret for the first $T$ rounds, no-regret means $\limsup_{T \to \infty} R_T/T \le 0$.} as $T \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Regret: gap between the best fixed $k$-set in hindsight and the protocol's reward; no-regret if average regret tends to 0.

nodes.name: Single-sensor case is the multiarmed bandit problem
nodes.statement: When $\ensuremath{k}=1$, our problem is simply the well-studied \emph{multiarmed bandit} (MAB) problem, for which many no-regret algorithms are known \cite{foster99}.

nodes.name: Greedy is $(1-1/e)$-approximate for the offline online-objective
nodes.statement: For general $\ensuremath{k}$, because the average of several submodular functions remains submodular, we can apply the result of Nemhauser~\emph{et al.}\~\cite{nemhauser78} (\emph{cf.}, Sec.~\ref{sec:offline-problem}) to prove that a simple greedy algorithm obtains a $(1-1/e)$ approximation to the optimal offline solution.
assumptions: general $\ensuremath{k}$
conclusions:
a simple greedy algorithm obtains a $(1-1/e)$
approximation to the optimal offline solution

nodes.name: Feige's $(1-1/e)$ hardness of approximation
nodes.statement: Feige~\cite{feige97} showed that this is optimal in the sense that obtaining a \\$(1-1/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for any $\epsilon > 0$ is \class{NP}-hard.
assumptions: any $\epsilon > 0$
conclusions:
obtaining a \\$(1-1/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for any $\epsilon > 0$ is
\class{NP}-hard

nodes.name: $(1-1/e)$-regret
nodes.statement: We therefore define the $(1-1/e)$-regret of a sequence of (possibly random) sets $\set{S_t}_{t=1}^T$ as \vspace{-0.5em} \[ \ensuremath{R}_{T} := \paren{1-1/e} \cdot \max_{S \subseteq V: |S| \le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S) \ - \ \sum_{t=1}^T \E{\ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)} \] where the expectation is taken over the distribution for each $S_t$.
nodes.statement_short: $R_T$: $(1-1/e)$ times the best fixed $k$-set's total reward minus the algorithm's expected total reward.

nodes.name: No-$(1-1/e)$-regret
nodes.statement: We say an online algorithm producing a sequence of sets has \emph{no-$(1-1/e)$-regret} if $\limsup_{T \to \infty} \frac{\ensuremath{R}_{T}}{T} \le 0$.

nodes.name: EXP3
nodes.statement: {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace works as follows: It is parameterized by a \emph{learning rate} $\eta$, and an \emph{exploration probability} $\gamma$. It maintains a set of weights $w_{s}$, one for each arm (sensor) $s$, initialized to 1. At every round $t$, it will select each arm $s$ with probability $$p_{s}=(1-\gamma)\frac{w_{s}}{\sum_{s'} w_{s'}}+\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}},$$ i.e., with probability $\gamma$ it explores, picking an arm uniformly at random, and with probability $(1-\gamma)$ it exploits, picking an arm $s$ with probability proportional to its weight $w_{s}$. Once an arm $s$ has been selected, a feedback $r=\ensuremath{f}_{t}(\{s\})$ is obtained, and the weight $w_{s}$ is updated to $$w_{s}\leftarrow w_{s}\exp(\eta r/p_{s}).$$
nodes.statement_short: Exponential-weights bandit algorithm: sample arms from a mixture of normalized weights and uniform exploration, then reweight the chosen arm by its importance-weighted reward.

nodes.name: Initialize weights
nodes.statement: It maintains a set of weights $w_{s}$, one for each arm (sensor) $s$, initialized to 1.

nodes.name: Sample an arm
nodes.statement: At every round $t$, it will select each arm $s$ with probability $$p_{s}=(1-\gamma)\frac{w_{s}}{\sum_{s'} w_{s'}}+\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}},$$ i.e., with probability $\gamma$ it explores, picking an arm uniformly at random, and with probability $(1-\gamma)$ it exploits, picking an arm $s$ with probability proportional to its weight $w_{s}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick arm $s$ w.p. $(1-\gamma)w_s/\sum w + \gamma/n$.

nodes.name: Observe feedback
nodes.statement: Once an arm $s$ has been selected, a feedback $r=\ensuremath{f}_{t}(\{s\})$ is obtained

nodes.name: Exponential weight update
nodes.statement: the weight $w_{s}$ is updated to $$w_{s}\leftarrow w_{s}\exp(\eta r/p_{s}).$$

nodes.name: EXP3 regret bound (Auer et al.)
nodes.statement: Auer et al.~\cite{auer02} showed that with appropriately chosen learning rate $\eta$ and exploration probability $\gamma$ it holds that the cumulative regret $R_{T}$ of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T \ensuremath{n} \ln \ensuremath{n} })$, i.e., the average regret $R_{T}/T$ converges to zero.
assumptions:
with appropriately chosen learning rate $\eta$ and exploration
probability $\gamma$
conclusions:
the cumulative regret $R_{T}$ of
{\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T \ensuremath{n} \ln \ensuremath{n} })$

nodes.name: Distributed sampling from a distribution
nodes.statement: The key challenge in developing a distributed version of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace is to find a way to sample exactly one element from a probability distribution $p$ over sensors in a distributed manner.
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor

nodes.name: Naive distributed sampling scheme
nodes.statement: A naive distributed algorithm would be to let each sensor keep track of all activation probabilities $p$. Then, one sensor (e.g., with the lowest identifier) would broadcast a single random number $u$ uniformly distributed in $[0,1]$, and the sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ for which $\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{v}-1} p_{i} \le u < \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{v}} p_{i}$ would activate.

nodes.name: Symmetry argument with fictitious sensors
nodes.statement: To improve upon the simple protocol, first consider running it on an example with $p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_n = 1/n$. Since the protocol behaves exactly the same under permutations of sensor labels, by symmetry we have $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{1} = \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{2} = \cdots = \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{n}$, and thus $r_i = r_j$ for all $i,j$. Now consider an input distribution $p$ where there exists integers $N$ and $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_n$ such that $p_{\ensuremath{v}} = k_{\ensuremath{v}}/N$ for all $\ensuremath{v}$. Replace each $\ensuremath{v}$ with $k_{\ensuremath{v}}$ fictitious sensors, each with probability mass $1/N$, and each with a label indicating $\ensuremath{v}$. Run the simple protocol with the fictitious sensors, selecting a fictitious sensor $\ensuremath{v}'$, and then actually select the sensor indicated by the label of $\ensuremath{v}'$. By symmetry this process selects each fictitious sensor with probability $(1-\ensuremath{\beta})/N$, where $\ensuremath{\beta}$ is the probability that nothing at all is selected, and thus the process selects sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability $k_{\ensuremath{v}}(1-\ensuremath{\beta})/N = (1-\ensuremath{\beta})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ (since at most one fictitious sensor is ever selected).
nodes.section: 4.1 Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor
nodes.statement_short: Splitting each sensor into $k_v$ fictitious sensors of mass $1/N$ and using symmetry makes the Simple Protocol select $v$ with probability $(1-\beta)p_v$.

nodes.name: Oversampling and the Poisson limit
nodes.statement: Assuming the probabilities are rational, there will be a sufficiently large $N$ to satisfy this condition. To reduce $\ensuremath{\beta} := \prob{S = \emptyset}$ in the simple protocol, we may sample each $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ from $\Bernoulli{\alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$ for any $\alpha \in [1, n]$. The symmetry argument remains unchanged. This in turn suggests sampling $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ from $\Binomial{\ceil{N \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}, \alpha/N}$ in the improved protocol. Taking the limit as $N \to \infty$, the binomial distribution becomes Poisson, and we obtain the desired protocol.

nodes.name: Robustness to estimates of $n$
nodes.statement: Running our variant of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace requires that each sensor know the number of sensors, $n$, in order to compute its activation probability. If each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ has only a reasonable estimate of $n_{\ensuremath{v}}$ of $n$, however, our algorithm still performs well. For example, it is possible to prove that if all of the sensors have the same estimate $n_{\ensuremath{v}} = cn$ for some constant $c > 0$, then the upper bound on expected regret, $R(c)$, grows as $R(c) \approx R(1)\cdot \max \set{c, 1/c}$. The expected number of activations in this case increases by at most $\paren{\frac{1}{c} - 1}\gamma$. In general underestimating $n$ leads to more activations, and underestimating or overestimating $n$ can lead to more regret. This graceful degradation of performance with respect to the error in estimating $n$ holds for all of our algorithms.

(Include $\ensuremath{v} \in S$ for convenience).\\ \If{$\ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}) = \min_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}')$}{ Select exactly one element $v_{it}$ from $S$ such that each $\ensuremath{v}'$ is selected with probability $X_{\ensuremath{v}'}/\sum_{u \in S} X_{u}$.\\ Broadcast $\tuple{\text{select } \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$.\\ } Receive message $\tuple{\text{select } \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$.\\ \If{$\ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}) = \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})$}{ Observe $\ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v})$; $\ensuremath{\pi} \gets \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v}) - \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t})$; $\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets w_{\ensuremath{v},i} (\exp\set{\eta \cdot \ensuremath{\pi}/ \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v},i}, Z_{\ensuremath{v},i})} - 1)$; $Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} + \Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}} + \Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$; Broadcast $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v})}$.\\ } } \lIf{\emph{receive message $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$}}{ $S_{\ensuremath{v},t} \gets S_{\ensuremath{v},t} \cup \set{\ensuremath{v}_{it}}$; $Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} + \Delta $;\\ } }

nodes.statement: Sample $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Poisson{\alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v},i}, Z_{\ensuremath{v},i})} $.

nodes.name: If activated
nodes.statement: \If{$(X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1)$} { Broadcast $\tuple{\text{sampled } X_{\ensuremath{v}}, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v})}$; Receive messages from sensors $S$. (Include $\ensuremath{v} \in S$ for convenience).\\ \If{$\ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}) = \min_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}')$}{ Select exactly one element $v_{it}$ from $S$ such that each $\ensuremath{v}'$ is selected with probability $X_{\ensuremath{v}'}/\sum_{u \in S} X_{u}$.\\ Broadcast $\tuple{\text{select } \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$.\\ } Receive message $\tuple{\text{select } \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$.\\ \If{$\ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}) = \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})$}{ Observe $\ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v})$; $\ensuremath{\pi} \gets \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v}) - \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t})$; $\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets w_{\ensuremath{v},i} (\exp\set{\eta \cdot \ensuremath{\pi}/ \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v},i}, Z_{\ensuremath{v},i})} - 1)$; $Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} + \Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}} + \Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$; Broadcast $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v})}$.\\ } }

nodes.statement: Broadcast $\tuple{\text{sampled } X_{\ensuremath{v}}, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v})}$; Receive messages from sensors $S$. (Include $\ensuremath{v} \in S$ for convenience).

nodes.name: Minimum-id sensor selects
nodes.statement: \If{$\ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}) = \min_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}')$}{ Select exactly one element $v_{it}$ from $S$ such that each $\ensuremath{v}'$ is selected with probability $X_{\ensuremath{v}'}/\sum_{u \in S} X_{u}$.\\ Broadcast $\tuple{\text{select } \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$.\\ }

nodes.name: Proportional selection
nodes.statement: Select exactly one element $v_{it}$ from $S$ such that each $\ensuremath{v}'$ is selected with probability $X_{\ensuremath{v}'}/\sum_{u \in S} X_{u}$.

nodes.name: Broadcast selection
nodes.statement: Broadcast $\tuple{\text{select } \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$.

nodes.name: Receive selection
nodes.statement: Receive message $\tuple{\text{select } \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$.

nodes.name: Selected sensor updates
nodes.statement: \If{$\ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}) = \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})$}{ Observe $\ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v})$; $\ensuremath{\pi} \gets \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v}) - \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t})$; $\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets w_{\ensuremath{v},i} (\exp\set{\eta \cdot \ensuremath{\pi}/ \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v},i}, Z_{\ensuremath{v},i})} - 1)$; $Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} + \Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}} + \Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$; Broadcast $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v})}$.\\ }

nodes.statement: Observe $\ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v})$; $\ensuremath{\pi} \gets \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t} + \ensuremath{v}) - \ensuremath{f}_t(S_{\ensuremath{v},t})$; $\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets w_{\ensuremath{v},i} (\exp\set{\eta \cdot \ensuremath{\pi}/ \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v},i}, Z_{\ensuremath{v},i})} - 1)$;
nodes.statement_short: Observe the marginal gain $\pi$ and compute the EXP3 weight increment $\Delta_v$.

nodes.name: Update normalizer and weight
nodes.statement: $Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} + \Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$;

nodes.name: Broadcast weight update
nodes.statement: Broadcast $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta_{\ensuremath{v}}, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v})}$.

nodes.name: Others record selection and update normalizer
nodes.statement: \lIf{\emph{receive message $\tuple{\text{weight update }\Delta, \ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v}_{it})}$}}{ $S_{\ensuremath{v},t} \gets S_{\ensuremath{v},t} \cup \set{\ensuremath{v}_{it}}$; $Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v},i} + \Delta $;\\ }

nodes.name: Sensors communicate only with the base station
nodes.statement: Every sensor stores its probability mass $p_\ensuremath{v}$ with it, and can only send messages to and receive messages from the base station.

nodes.name: Base station computes utilities
nodes.statement: The base station is able, after receiving messages from a set $S$ of sensors, to compute the utility $\ensuremath{f}_{t}(S)$ and send this utility back to the active sensors.

nodes.name: Normalizer $Z(t)$
nodes.statement: In {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace, each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ requires only $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ and a normalizer $Z(t) :=\sum_{\ensuremath{v}'}w_{\ensuremath{v}'}(t)$ to compute $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$\footnote{We let $x(t)$ denote the value of variable $x$ at the start of round $t$, to ease analysis. We do not actually need to store the historical values of the variables over multiple time steps.}.

nodes.name: Normalizer estimates $Z_v(t)$
nodes.statement: Each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ maintains its weight $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ and an estimate $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ for $Z(t) := \sum_{\ensuremath{v}'}w_{\ensuremath{v}'}(t)$, Initially, $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(0) = 1$ and $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(0) = \ensuremath{n}$ for all $\ensuremath{v}$.

nodes.name: Sampling map $\rho$
nodes.statement: Let \[ \rho(x, y) := (1-\gamma)\frac{x}{y} + \frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}\mbox{.} \]

nodes.name: Lazy probability estimate $q_v$
nodes.statement: Each sensor then proceeds to activate as in the sampling procedure of~Sec.~\ref{sec:sampling} as if its probability mass in round $t$ were $q_{\ensuremath{v}} = \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$ instead of its true value of $\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$.

nodes.name: Distributed EXP3 activation and message bounds
nodes.statement: The number of sensor activations in any round of the Distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace algorithm is at most \mbox{$\alpha + (e-1)$} in expectation and $\mathcal{O}(\alpha + \log n)$ with high probability, and the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations.
assumptions: any round of the Distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace algorithm
conclusions:
The number of sensor activations in any round of the Distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace algorithm 
is at most \mbox{$\alpha + (e-1)$} in
expectation and $\mathcal{O}(\alpha + \log n)$ with high probability
the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations
nodes.label: thm:dexp3-performance

nodes.name: Setting $\alpha = c\ln n$ and rerunning
nodes.statement: Unfortunately, there is still an $e^{-\alpha}$ probability of nothing being selected. To address this, we can set $\alpha = c\ln n$ for some $c \ge 1$, and if nothing is selected, transmit a message to each of the $n$ sensors to rerun the protocol.

nodes.name: Distributed EXP3 with guaranteed selection
nodes.statement: There is a distributed implementation of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace that always selects a sensor in each round, has the same regret bounds as standard {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace, ensures that the number of sensor activations in any round is at most $\ln n + \mathcal{O}(1)$ in expectation or $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ with high probability, and in which the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations.
conclusions:
There is a distributed implementation of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace that always selects a
sensor in each round, has the same regret bounds as standard
{\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace
nodes.statement_short: A distributed EXP3 always selects a sensor, matches EXP3's regret, and uses $\ln n+O(1)$ expected activations and at most twice as many messages.
nodes.label: cor:dexp3-performance

nodes.name: Distributed EXP3 (lazy renormalization)
nodes.statement: \Titleofalgo { Distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace (executing on round $t$)} \KwIn{Parameters $\alpha, \eta, \gamma \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}_{> 0}$, sensor set $V$.} Let $\rho(x, y) := (1-\gamma)\frac{x}{y} + \frac{\gamma}{|V|}$.\\ \emph{Sensors: } \\ \For {\KwEach \emph{sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ in parallel}}{ Sample $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.\\ \If {$(r_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$}{ Send $\tuple{r_{\ensuremath{v}}, w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}$ to the server.\\ Receive message $\tuple{Z, w}$ from server.\\ $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets Z$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets w$. \\ }\lElse{ $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.\\ } } \emph{Server:}\\ Receive messages from a set $S$ of sensors. \\ \lIf{$S = \emptyset$}{Select nothing and wait for next round.} \lElse{ \For {\KwEach \emph{sensor} $\ensuremath{v} \in S$}{ $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets \min \set{x : \prob{X \le x} \ge r_{\ensuremath{v}}}$, where $X \sim \Poisson{\alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),Z(t))}$.\\ Select $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}/\sum_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} Y_{\ensuremath{v}'}$.\\ Observe the payoff $\ensuremath{\pi}$ for the selected sensor $\ensuremath{v}^*$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t) \cdot \exp \set{\eta \ensuremath{\pi} / \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t),Z(t))}$; $Z(t+1) \gets Z(t) + w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t+1) - w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t)$\; \lFor{ \KwEach $\ensuremath{v} \in S \setminus \ensuremath{v}^*$}{ $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$\; } \lFor{ \KwEach $\ensuremath{v} \!\in\! S$}{ Send $\tuple{Z(t\!+\!1), w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t\!+\!1)}$ to $\ensuremath{v}$.\\ } } } \caption{Distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace: the PMS Protocol($\alpha$) with lazy renormalization, applied to {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace}
nodes.statement_short: PMS Protocol with lazy renormalization applied to EXP3: sensors activate using stale normalizer estimates; the server resamples Poisson counts with the true normalizer, selects and updates.

nodes.statement: Send $\tuple{r_{\ensuremath{v}}, w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}$ to the server.

nodes.name: Receive from server
nodes.statement: Receive message $\tuple{Z, w}$ from server.

nodes.name: Refresh local state
nodes.statement: $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets Z$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets w$.

nodes.name: Otherwise keep state
nodes.statement: \lElse{ $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.\\ }

nodes.statement: Receive messages from a set $S$ of sensors.

nodes.name: Nothing activated
nodes.statement: \lIf{$S = \emptyset$}{Select nothing and wait for next round.}

nodes.name: Otherwise process active sensors
nodes.statement: \lElse{ \For {\KwEach \emph{sensor} $\ensuremath{v} \in S$}{ $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets \min \set{x : \prob{X \le x} \ge r_{\ensuremath{v}}}$, where $X \sim \Poisson{\alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),Z(t))}$.\\ Select $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}/\sum_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} Y_{\ensuremath{v}'}$.\\ Observe the payoff $\ensuremath{\pi}$ for the selected sensor $\ensuremath{v}^*$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t) \cdot \exp \set{\eta \ensuremath{\pi} / \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t),Z(t))}$; $Z(t+1) \gets Z(t) + w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t+1) - w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t)$\; \lFor{ \KwEach $\ensuremath{v} \in S \setminus \ensuremath{v}^*$}{ $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$\; } \lFor{ \KwEach $\ensuremath{v} \!\in\! S$}{ Send $\tuple{Z(t\!+\!1), w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t\!+\!1)}$ to $\ensuremath{v}$.\\ } } }

nodes.statement: \For {\KwEach \emph{sensor} $\ensuremath{v} \in S$}{ $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets \min \set{x : \prob{X \le x} \ge r_{\ensuremath{v}}}$, where $X \sim \Poisson{\alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),Z(t))}$.\\ Select $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}/\sum_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} Y_{\ensuremath{v}'}$.\\ Observe the payoff $\ensuremath{\pi}$ for the selected sensor $\ensuremath{v}^*$; $w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t) \cdot \exp \set{\eta \ensuremath{\pi} / \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t),Z(t))}$; $Z(t+1) \gets Z(t) + w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t+1) - w_{\ensuremath{v}^*}(t)$\; \lFor{ \KwEach $\ensuremath{v} \in S \setminus \ensuremath{v}^*$}{ $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \gets w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$\; } \lFor{ \KwEach $\ensuremath{v} \!\in\! S$}{ Send $\tuple{Z(t\!+\!1), w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t\!+\!1)}$ to $\ensuremath{v}$.\\ } }

nodes.statement: $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \gets \min \set{x : \prob{X \le x} \ge r_{\ensuremath{v}}}$, where $X \sim \Poisson{\alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),Z(t))}$.

nodes.name: Proportional selection
nodes.statement: Select $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}/\sum_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} Y_{\ensuremath{v}'}$.

nodes.name: Observe payoff and update weight and normalizer

nodes.statement: \lFor{ \KwEach $\ensuremath{v} \!\in\! S$}{ Send $\tuple{Z(t\!+\!1), w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t\!+\!1)}$ to $\ensuremath{v}$.\\ }

nodes.name: lazyDOG
nodes.statement: Once we have the distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace variant described above, we can use it for the bandit subroutines in the $\algofont{OG}_{\algofont{unit}}$\xspace algorithm (\emph{cf.}~Sec.~\ref{sec:centralized-multi}). We call the result the \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace algorithm, due to its use of lazy renormalization.
nodes.statement_short: OG_unit with Distributed EXP3 (lazy renormalization) as the per-stage bandit subroutine.

nodes.name: lazyDOG has DOG's guarantees
nodes.statement: The lazy distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace still samples sensors from the same distribution as the regular distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace, so \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace has precisely the same performance guarantees with respect to $\sum_{t} \ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$ as \algofont{DOG}\xspace.

The lazy distributed
{\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace still samples sensors from the same distribution as the
regular distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace
conclusions:
\algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace has precisely the same
performance guarantees with respect to $\sum_{t} \ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$ as
\algofont{DOG}\xspace

nodes.name: lazyDOG activation, message and regret bounds
nodes.statement: The number of sensors that activate each round in \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace is at most $\ensuremath{k}\ln n + \mathcal{O}(\ensuremath{k})$ in expectation and $\mathcal{O}(\ensuremath{k}\log n)$ with high probability, the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations, and the $\paren{1 - 1/e}$-regret of \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace is the same as \algofont{DOG}\xspace.
conclusions:
The number of sensors that activate each round in 
\algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace is at most $\ensuremath{k}\ln n + \mathcal{O}(\ensuremath{k})$ in expectation and 
$\mathcal{O}(\ensuremath{k}\log n)$ with high probability
the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations
the $\paren{1 - 1/e}$-regret of \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace is the same as \algofont{DOG}\xspace
nodes.label: cor:lazydog-performance

nodes.name: lazyDOG without reruns ($k'$ stages)
nodes.statement: If we are not concerned about the exact number of sensors selected in each round, but only want to ensure roughly $\ensuremath{k}$ sensors are picked in expectation, then we can reduce the number of sensor activations and messages to $\mathcal{O}(\ensuremath{k})$, by running \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace with $\ensuremath{k}' := \ceil{\ensuremath{k}/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ stages for some constant $\alpha$, and allowing each stage to run the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace with lazy renormalization \emph{without} rerunning it if nothing is selected.
nodes.statement_short: Run lazyDOG for $k'=\lceil k/(1-e^{-\alpha})\rceil$ stages without rerunning empty stages, giving $O(k)$ activations.

nodes.name: Run lazyDOG with $k'$ stages
nodes.statement: running \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace with $\ensuremath{k}' := \ceil{\ensuremath{k}/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ stages for some constant $\alpha$

nodes.name: No rerun on empty stages
nodes.statement: allowing each stage to run the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace with lazy renormalization \emph{without} rerunning it if nothing is selected

nodes.name: Optimality up to constants
nodes.statement: This is of course optimal up to constants, as we must send at least one message per selected sensor.
conclusions: This is of course optimal up to constants

nodes.name: lazyDOG variant guarantees
nodes.statement: The variant of \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace that runs the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace$(\alpha)$ with lazy renormalization for $\ensuremath{k}' := \ceil{\ensuremath{k}/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ stages, but does not rerun it if nothing is selected in a given stage, has the following guarantees: ($1$) the number of sensors that activate each round in \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace is at most $\ensuremath{k}' (\alpha + e -1)$ in expectation and $\mathcal{O}(\alpha\ensuremath{k}\log n)$ with high probability, ($2$) the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations, ($3$) the expected number of sensors selected in each round is at most $\ensuremath{k}'$ and $(4)$ its $\paren{1 - 1/e}$-regret is at most $\ensuremath{k}' / \ensuremath{k}$ times that of \algofont{DOG}\xspace.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 8
nodes.statement: Let $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Bernoulli{\alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$ be the indicator random variable for the activation of $\ensuremath{v}$, and let $X := \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} X_{\ensuremath{v}}$. The expected number of sensor activations is then \[ \E{X \ |\ X \ge 1} = \E{X}/\prob{X \ge 1} \mbox{.} \] In the limit as $\max_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ tends to zero, $X$ converges to a Poisson random variable with mean $\alpha$. In this case, $\frac{\E{X}}{\prob{X \ge 1}} = \alpha / (1 - e^{-\alpha})$ To see that this is an upper bound, consider an arbitrary distribution $p$ on the sensors, and fix some $\ensuremath{v}$ with $x := p_{\ensuremath{v}} > 0$. We claim that replacing $\ensuremath{v}$ with two sensors $\ensuremath{v}_1$ and $\ensuremath{v}_2$ with positive probability mass $x_1$ and $x_2$ with $x = x_1+x_2$ can only serve to increase the expected number of sensor activations, because $\E{X}$ is unchanged, and $\prob{X \ge 1}$ decreases. The latter is true essentially because $\prob{\exists i \in \set{1,2}: \ensuremath{v}_i \text{ activates}} = 1 - (1-x_1)(1-x_2) = x - x_1x_2 < x$. To complete the proof, notice that repeating this process with $\ensuremath{v} = \mathop{\rm arg\,max} (p_{\ensuremath{v}})$ and $x_i = x/2$ ensures $X$ converges to a Poisson variable with mean $\alpha$, while only increasing $\E{X \ |\ X \ge 1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 9
nodes.statement: Lazy renormalization selects each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability $(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, because of the way the random bits $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are shared in order to implement a coupled distribution for sensor activation and selection. Note that it would be sufficient to run the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace on the correct (possibly oversampled) probabilities, $\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, since then~Prop.~\ref{thm:sampling} ensures that each $\ensuremath{v}$ is selected with probability $(1 - e^{-\alpha}) p_{\ensuremath{v}}$. The difficulty is that $\ensuremath{v}$ does not have access to the correct normalizer $Z(t)$, but only its estimate (lower bound) for it, $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$. To overcome this difficulty, we define a joint probability distribution over two random variables $(X_{\ensuremath{v}}, Y_{\ensuremath{v}})$, where \[ X_{\ensuremath{v}} = X_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1 & \text{if $R \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{array} \right. \] \[ Y_{\ensuremath{v}} = Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \min \set{b \ :\ \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^{a}}{a!} \ge R } \] and $\lambda := \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$, and $R$ is sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$. Now, note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}$ is distributed as $\Poisson{\lambda}$. Also note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$, because $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $R \ge e^{-\lambda}$ and \[ e^{-\lambda} \ge 1 - \lambda \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)) \] since $1 + x \le e^x$ for all $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, and $\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)) \ge \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$ due to fact that $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \le Z(t)$. It follows that we can use the event $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ as a conservative indicator that $\ensuremath{v}$ should activate. In this case, it will send its sampled value for $R$, namely $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$, and its weight $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to the server. The server knows $Z(t)$, and then can use $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ and $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to compute $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(r_{\ensuremath{v}})$, the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\ensuremath{v}$ would have drawn had it known $Z(t)$. The resulting distribution on selected sensors is thus exactly the same as in the Poisson Multinomial Sampling Protocol\xspace without lazy renormalization. Invoking~Prop.~\ref{thm:sampling} thus completes the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 10
nodes.statement: Fix $\ensuremath{v}$, and let $p(t) := p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$, $q(t) := q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$. We begin by bounding $\prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}$ for $\lambda \ge 1$. Let $t_0$ be the most recent round in which $q(t_0) = p(t_0)$. We assume $q(0) = p(0)$, so $t_0$ exists. Then $q(t) = p(t_0) \ge \lambda p(t)$ implies $p(t_0)/p(t) \ge \lambda$. By assumption $p(t')/p(t'+1) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t'$, so $p(t_0)/p(t) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$. Thus $\lambda \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$ and $t-t_0 \ge \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$. Define $t(\lambda) := \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$. By definition of $t_0$, there were no activations under lazy renormalization in rounds $t_0$ through $t-1$ inclusive, which occurs with probability $\prod_{t' = t_0}^{t-1} (1-\alpha q(t'))$ $=$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{t-t_{0}} $ $\le$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{\ceil{t(\lambda)}}$, where $\alpha$ is the oversampling parameter in the protocol. We now bound $\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)}$. Recall that $\E{X} = \int_{x = 0}^{\infty} \prob{X \ge x}dx$ for any non-negative random variable $X$. It will also be convenient to define $\ensuremath{\omega} := \ln(1/(1 - \alpha q(t))) / \ln(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ and assume for now that $\ensuremath{\omega} > 1$. Conditioning on $q(t)$, we see that \[ \begin{array}{lcl} \vspace{2mm} \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} & = & \int_{\lambda = 0}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & \le & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} (1-\alpha q(t))^{t(\lambda)}d\lambda\\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \lambda^{\ln(1-\alpha q(t))/\ln(1+\hat{\epsilon}) }d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \lambda^{-\ensuremath{\omega}}d\lambda \\ \vspace{2mm} & = & 1 + \frac{1}{\ensuremath{\omega} - 1} \end{array} \] Using $\ln\paren{\frac{1}{1-x}} \ge x$ for all $x < 1$ and $\ln(1+x) \le x$ for all $x > -1$, we can show that $\ensuremath{\omega} \ge \alpha q(t)/\hat{\epsilon}$ so $1+\frac{1}{\ensuremath{\omega} - 1} \le \alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$. Thus, if $\alpha q(t) > \hat{\epsilon}$ then $\ensuremath{\omega} > 1$ and we obtain $\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le \alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$. If $q(t) >> \hat{\epsilon}$, this gives a good bound. If $q(t)$ is small, we rely on the assumption that $p(t) \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$ to get a trivial bound of $q(t)/p(t) \le q(t)/\epsilon$. We thus conclude \begin{equation} \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le \min \paren{\alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon}) ,\ q(t)/\epsilon}\mbox{.} \end{equation} Setting $q(t) = (\hat{\epsilon}/\alpha + \epsilon)$ to maximize this quantity yields an unconditional bound of $\E{q(t)/p(t)} \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon$. To bound $\E{q(t)}$ in terms of $\E{p(t)}$, note that for all $q$ \begin{align*} q/\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q} & \le \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)=q}\\ & \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon \end{align*} where the first line is by Jensen's inequality, and the second is by equation~\ref{eqn:ratio-bound}. Thus $q \le \paren{1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon}\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q}$ for all $q$. Taking the expectation with respect to $q$ then proves $\E{q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} \le \paren{1 + \frac{\hat{\epsilon}}{\alpha\epsilon}} \E{p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}$ as claimed.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: The former equality is an easy observation. To prove the latter equality, fix a round $t$ and a selected action $\ensuremath{v}$. Let $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ be the weight of $\ensuremath{v}$ in round $t$, and $W(t)$ be the total weight of all actions in round $t$. Let $\ensuremath{\pi}$ be the payoff to $\ensuremath{v}$ in round $t$. Given the update rule $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) = w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)\exp\paren{\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}\frac{\ensuremath{\pi}(\ensuremath{v},t)}{p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}}$, only the probabilities of the other actions will be decreased. It is not hard to see that they will be decreased by a multiplicative factor of at most $W(t)/W(t+1)$, no matter what the learning parameter $\gamma$ is. By the update rule, \[ W(t+1) = W(t) + w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)\paren{\exp\paren{\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}} \frac{\ensuremath{\pi}}{p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}} - 1}\mbox{.} \] Let $p := p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ and $x := \frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}\ensuremath{\pi}$. Dividing the above equation by $W(t)$, we get \begin{align} \frac{W(t+1)}{W(t)} & = 1 + p\paren{\exp\paren{x/p} - 1} \\ & \le 1 + p\paren{x/p + (e-2)(x/p)^2}\\ & \le 1 + x + (e-2)x^2/p \end{align} where in the second line we have used $e^x \le 1 + x + (e-2)x^2$ for $x \in [0,1]$. Note $\ensuremath{\pi} \le 1$ implies $x \le \gamma/n \le p$, so $\frac{W(t+1)}{W(t)} \le 1 + (e-1)x \le 1 + (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$. It follows that setting $\hat{\epsilon} = (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$ is sufficient to ensure $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \ge p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)/(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: We prove in Lemma~\ref{lem:exp3conditions} that {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace satisfies the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} with $\epsilon = \gamma/\ensuremath{n}$ and $\hat{\epsilon} = (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$. Thus by Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} \begin{align*} \E{\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} & \le \paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}\E{\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}\\ & = \paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha} \end{align*} because $\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) = 1$. Each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ activates with probability $\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$, so the expected number of activations is \[ \E{\alpha \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} \le \alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}\mbox{.} \] That proves the claimed bounds in expectation. To prove bounds with high probability, note that a sensor activates with probability $\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ in round $t$, where $q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ is a random variable. Fix $t$. Let $[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}]$ denote the indicator variable for the event $\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}$, i.e., $[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}] = 1$ if $\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}$ occurs, and $[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}] = 0$ otherwise. Then we can write $[\ensuremath{v} \text{ activates in round }t] = [\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge R]$, where $R$ is sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$ and $R$ is independent of $q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$. Then if $f_R$ is the probability density functions of $R$ we can write \[ \begin{aligned} \prob{R \le \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge R \ |\ R = r} f_R(r) dr\\ & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge r} f_R(r) dr \\ & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge r}dr \\ & = \E{ \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) } \end{aligned} \] Thus the number of sensor activations is a sum of $|V|$ binary random variables with cumulative mean $\mu := \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \E{ \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) }$. We have already bounded this mean as $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$. From here a simple application of a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound suffices to prove that with high probability this sum is at most $\mathcal{O}(\alpha + \log n)$. Let $A$ be the number of sensor activations. Then, e.g., Theorem~$5$ of~\cite{CL06} immediately implies \[ \prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{\delta^2 \mu^2}{2 \mu + \frac{2\delta \mu}{3}}} \] For $\delta \ge 1$, this yields $\prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{3\delta\mu}{8}}$. Setting $\delta = 1 + \frac{8c\ln n}{3\mu}$ ensures this probability is at most $n^{-c}$, hence $\prob{A \ge 2\mu + \frac{8}{3}c\ln n} \le n^{-c}$. Noting that $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$ completes the high probability bound on the number of activations. As for the number of messages, note that each message involves a sensor as sender or receiver, and by inspection the protocol only involves two messages per activated node.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5
nodes.statement: Use the distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace protocol with lazy renormalization with $\alpha = \ln n$. We have already established that the probability of nothing being selected is $e^{-\alpha}$ or $1/n$ in this case. If nothing is selected, send out $n$ messages, one to each sensor, to rerun the protocol. The expected number of messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol is $\sum_{x=1}^{\infty} nx/n^{x} = \paren{1 - 1/n}^{-2} = 1 + \mathcal{O}(1/n)$. Let $X$ be the number of sensor activations. As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:broadcast-activations}, if $Y$ is the expected number of sensor activations without rerunning the protocol when nothing is selected, then $\E{X} = \E{Y}/\prob{Y \ge 1}$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance} $\E{Y} \le \alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}$. Since $\prob{Y \ge 1} = 1 - e^{-\alpha}$, we conclude \[ \E{X} \le \ln n + (e-1) + \mathcal{O}\paren{\frac{\ln n}{n}}\mbox{.} \] The with-high-probability bounds on the number of sensor activations are proved as in the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:dexp3-performance}. As for the number of messages, note that other than messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol, there are only two messages per activated node. Finally, the regret bounds for distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace are the same as standard {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace because by design the two algorithms select sensors from exactly the same distribution in each round. Note that the distribution in any given round is a random object depending on the algorithm's choices in the previous rounds, however on each round the distribution on distributions is the same for both {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace variants, as can be readily proved by induction on the round number.

nodes.statement: We claim that we can compensate for this possibility by running \algofont{DOG}\xspace for $\ensuremath{k}/(1-\delta)$ stages in each round rather than $\ensuremath{k}$, because of the following guarantee for $\algofont{OG}_{\algofont{unit}}$\xspace.

nodes.name: $\algofont{OG}_{\algofont{unit}}$ with faulty actions
nodes.statement: Fix finite set $V$, $\ensuremath{k} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, and a sequence of monotone submodular functions $f_1, \ldots, f_T:2^{V} \to [0,1]$. Let $\textsf{OPT}_{\ensuremath{k}} = \max_{S \subset V, |S| \le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^{t} f_t(S)$. For all $\ensuremath{v} \in V$ let $\ensuremath{v}'$ be a random element which is $v$ with probability $1-\delta_\ensuremath{v}$ and is $\textsf{null}$\footnote{Here, a $\textsf{null}$ element always contributes nothing in the way of utility, so that $f_t(S \cup \set{\textsf{null}}) = f_t(S)$ for all $t$ and $S$.} with probability $\delta_\ensuremath{v}$. Let $f'_t(S') := \E{f_t(S)}$ where $S$ the set obtained by including every element $\ensuremath{v}'$ of $S'$ in it independently with probability $\delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$. Let $S'_1, \ldots, S'_T$ be the sequence of random sets obtained from running $\algofont{OG}_{\algofont{unit}}$\xspace with actions $V' := \set{\ensuremath{v}' : \ensuremath{v} \in V}$ and objective functions $\set{f'_t}_{t = 1}^T$ and $\ensuremath{k}' = \ensuremath{k}/(1-\delta)$ stages, where $\delta = \max_{\ensuremath{v}} \delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$. Suppose the algorithms for each stage have expected regret at most $r$. Then \[ \E{\sum_{t=1}^T f'_t(S'_t)} \ge \paren{1-\frac{1}{e}}\textsf{OPT}_{\ensuremath{k}} - \ceil{\frac{\ensuremath{k}}{1-\delta}} r\mbox{.} \]

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 11
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the analogous result in the offline case; the ``meta-actions'' analysis in~\cite{streeter07tr} can then be used to complete the proof. So consider a set of elements $V$ and the ``faulty'' versions $V'$. Fix a monotone submodular $f:2^{V} \to [0,1]$ and define $f'$ as above. Run the offline greedy algorithm on $f'$ to try to find the best set of $\ensuremath{k}' = \frac{\ensuremath{k}}{1-\delta}$ elements in $V'$. Let $g'_i$ be the chosen element in stage $i$, and let $G'_i = \set{g'_j : 1 \le j \le i}$. Let $G_i$ denote the realization of $G'_i$ after sampling, so that $G_i \subseteq \set{g : g' \in G'_i}$. Let $S^* = \mathop{\rm arg\,max}_{S \subseteq V, |S| \le \ensuremath{k}}(f(S))$. We claim that for all $i$ \[ \Econd{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)}{G_i} \ge \paren{1-\delta} \frac{f(S^*) - f(G_i)}{\ensuremath{k}} \] because \begin{align*} f(S^*) - f(G_i) & \le f(G_i \cup S^*) - f(G_i)\\ & \le \sum_{\ensuremath{v} \in S^*} \paren{f(G_i + \ensuremath{v}) - f(G_i)}\\ & \le \ensuremath{k} \cdot \max_{\ensuremath{v}} \paren{f(G_i + \ensuremath{v}) - f(G_i)} \end{align*} and $\max_{\ensuremath{v}'} \paren{\Econd{f(G'_i + \ensuremath{v}') - f(G'_i)}{G_i} }$ is at least equal to $(1-\delta)\max_{\ensuremath{v}} \paren{f(G_i + \ensuremath{v}) - f(G_i)}$. Removing the conditioning on $G_i$ we get \[ \E{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)} \ge \paren{1-\delta}\frac{f(S^*) - \E{f(G'_i)}}{\ensuremath{k}} \] Let $\Phi(i) = f(S^*) - \E{f(G'_{i})}$. The previous equation implies $\Phi(i+1) \le \Phi(i)\paren{1 - \frac{1-\delta}{\ensuremath{k}}}$. By induction $\Phi(i) \le f(S^*)\paren{1 - \frac{1-\delta}{\ensuremath{k}}}^i$. Using $1-x \le e^{-x}$ we conclude that $\Phi(\ceil{\ensuremath{k}/(1-\delta)}) \le f(S^*)/e$ and $f'(G_{\ensuremath{k}'}) \ge \paren{1-\frac{1}{e}}f(S^*)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the offline greedy case; each faulty greedy step closes a $(1-\delta)/k$ fraction of the gap, and induction gives $(1-1/e)$ after $k/(1-\delta)$ steps.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7
nodes.statement: To bound the number of sensor activations, we note there are $\ensuremath{k}' := \ceil{\ensuremath{k}/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ rounds, and each round activates at most $\alpha + (e-1)$ sensors in expectation and $\mathcal{O}(\alpha + \log n)$ sensors with high probability by Theorem~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance} (which proves these bounds in the higher communication case where we do rerun the PMS Protocol\xspace protocol if nothing is selected). This, and the fact that $\alpha/(1 - e^{-\alpha}) = O(\alpha)$ for $\alpha > 0$ yields the claimed activation bounds. It is an easy observation that the number of messages is at most twice the number of activations. Clearly, at most one sensor per stage is activated, so at most $\ensuremath{k}'$ are activated over one round. Finally, the regret bound follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:faulty-sensors}, using $\delta = e^{-\alpha}$.
